chunks: Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Sama'ah narrated from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan al-Mithami, from Aban ibn Uthman, from Abdullah ibn Muhrij, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who entrusted his affairs to me, then died, leaving a daughter. He said: 'Give the daughter half, and leave half for the mawali (clients/relatives by contract).'
So I returned to them, and they said: 'By Allah, the mawali have nothing (no share).'
So I returned to him the next time and said: 'Indeed, our companions said that the mawali have nothing.'

He said: 'I only feared for you.' I said: 'No, by Allah, you did not fear me, but you feared that I would be taken (held liable) for the half. If you do not fear, then give the other half to his daughter, for Allah will compensate you.'

key_terms.اَلْمَوَالِي: Mawali (clients or relatives by contract, often manumitted slaves or their descendants)
key_terms.تُؤْخَذَ: Taken/Held liable (in a legal or financial sense)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on the share of mawali in inheritance when a daughter is present?
ai.summary: This hadith illustrates the Shia juristic principle of *al-khawf min al-ruju'* (fear of reversion), where the Imam advises the narrator to withhold the mawali's share not because it is invalid, but to protect the narrator from potential litigation if the mawali later assert their right. This reflects the practical wisdom of *ihtiyat* (caution) in inheritance distribution, balancing strict legal entitlement with social prudence. The Imam’s assurance of divine compensation highlights the spiritual merit of bearing the risk of loss for the sake of clarity and peace.
